title: Impact of ChatGPT on ESL students’ academic writing skills: a mixed methods intervention study
extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether using ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool improves academic writing skills among ESL learners. The study is motivated by the difficulty of providing individualized feedback in large writing classes and by the limited empirical evidence on the effects of generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, on student writing. The research asks whether ChatGPT-based feedback has a significant impact on writing performance when instructional time and tasks are held constant, and how students perceive that impact.

The study used a mixed-methods intervention design with a comparison group. The experimental group received a short training session on using ChatGPT for self-assessment and peer assessment, then used ChatGPT during a six-hour instructional intervention focused on process, comparison, and cause-effect writing. The comparison group received the same writing instruction but without the ChatGPT-supported feedback process. Quantitative data came from pre-test, post-test, and delayed post-test writing assessments scored with validated rubrics covering content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary; qualitative data came from three focus group discussions with experimental-group students.

Participants were first-year science and engineering undergraduates at a private university in India, aged 18–19, all with English as a second language. Final analyzed samples included 35 students in the comparison group and 37 in the experimental group. The intervention occurred in regular university writing classes over about one month, with an additional delayed post-test roughly two months later.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT had a significant positive effect on students’ academic writing skills, with the experimental group outperforming the comparison group on both immediate and delayed post-tests. Students also reported largely positive experiences, especially for idea generation, organization, grammar support, and collaborative revision, though some expressed concerns about overdependence and reduced creativity. The author argues that, with training, ChatGPT can function as an effective formative feedback tool in large ESL writing classes, while noting limitations related to genre coverage, short intervention time, lack of artifact analysis, and constrained generalizability.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental mixed-methods intervention study with a comparison group, pre/post/delayed post testing, reported statistical tests, and rubric-based scoring with strong inter-rater reliability (kappa > 0.8). However, it is not an RCT, uses an intact university sample, and is not directly relevant to grades 9-12 secondary students.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported writing effects are large and consistently positive, including η²=0.902 and very large within-group gains, with significant advantages over the comparison group at post-test and delayed post-test. Despite relevance limitations for K-12, the magnitude of impact in the studied population is clearly medium-to-large.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT used as a formative feedback tool for undergraduate ESL academic paragraph writing, supporting self-assessment and peer-assessment on content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary during process, comparison, and cause-effect writing tasks.
ChatGPT used dialogically as a conversational feedback assistant that answers student queries, explains grammar, suggests revisions, and supports brainstorming during writing instruction.

finding.finding_summary: In this quasi-experimental mixed-methods study of undergraduate ESL students, the ChatGPT intervention group outperformed the comparison group on academic writing quality after the intervention and at delayed post-test. For the experimental group, repeated-measures ANOVA showed significant gains across pre-, post-, and delayed post-tests (F[2,72]=330.704, p=5.146e-37, η²=0.902); Bonferroni comparisons showed large gains from pre- to post-test (d=-3.300) and pre- to delayed post-test (d=-3.898), with an additional post- to delayed gain (d=-0.598). Between groups, post-test scores favored the ChatGPT group (EG M=19.216, SD=2.485, n=37 vs CG M=16.371, SD=1.695, n=35; t[70]=-5.643, p=3.297e-7) and delayed post-test scores also favored the ChatGPT group (EG M=20.419, SD=2.575 vs CG M=15.400, SD=1.897; t[70]=-9.371, p=5.544e-14).
finding.measure: Rubric-scored academic writing tests assessing content, organization, grammar, and vocabulary across process, comparison, and cause-effect paragraph tasks
finding.study_size: n=72 analyzed total (EG n=37, CG n=35)
finding.effect_size: η²=0.902; within-EG Bonferroni pairwise d=-3.300, d=-3.898, d=-0.598
finding.std_deviation: EG post SD=2.485; EG delayed SD=2.575; CG post SD=1.695; CG delayed SD=1.897

finding.finding_summary: Qualitative focus-group evidence suggested that students perceived ChatGPT-supported self- and peer-assessment as improving autonomy, collaboration, and metalinguistic reflection during writing. Students reported more independent problem-solving, more peer discussion around revisions, and stronger awareness of how ideas and grammatical choices connect, though some also worried about overdependence and reduced creativity.
finding.measure: Focus group discussions on learner autonomy, collaboration, self-/peer-assessment, and reflection during writing revision

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT reduced brainstorming time, enabled faster writing-task completion, and provided on-demand feedback in large classes where individualized human feedback is difficult. These efficiency findings were qualitative and based on participant perceptions rather than direct time-on-task or workload measurements.
finding.measure: Focus group perceptions of writing speed, time-saving, and feedback availability in large-class contexts
